blocks.es_reference: 📖 Predicación Doctrinal — Unidad 3: Predicando la Doctrina de la Revelación

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "God... has in these last days spoken to us by His Son." — Hebrews 1:1–2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Dios... en estos postreros días nos ha hablado por el Hijo." — Hebreos 1:1–2 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 1 — Why Preach Revelation First?
blocks.es_reference: Día 1 — ¿Por qué predicar primero la Revelación?

blocks.en: With Unit 3 the course turns from method to the doctrines themselves, and it begins where theology itself begins: with revelation. This order is deliberate. Before a preacher can say anything about who God is (Unit 4), he must settle how anyone can know — and the answer is that God has spoken. Revelation is the doctrine that makes every other sermon possible.
blocks.es_reference: Con la Unidad 3 el curso pasa del método a las doctrinas mismas, y comienza donde comienza la teología misma: con la revelación. Este orden es deliberado. Antes de que un predicador pueda decir algo sobre quién es Dios (Unidad 4), debe resolver cómo puede alguien conocerlo — y la respuesta es que Dios ha hablado. La revelación es la doctrina que hace posible todo otro sermón.

blocks.en: So the preacher’s aim in this unit is pastoral before it is academic. The sermon on revelation must move the hearer from religion as a human search — man reaching up, guessing, hoping — to faith as a response to a God who has already spoken. The good news is not that we have found God; it is that God has made Himself known.
blocks.es_reference: Así que el objetivo del predicador en esta unidad es pastoral antes que académico. El sermón sobre la revelación debe mover al oyente de la religión como búsqueda humana — el hombre estirando la mano, adivinando, esperando — a la fe como respuesta a un Dios que ya ha hablado. La buena nueva no es que hayamos encontrado a Dios; es que Dios se ha dado a conocer.

blocks.en: "God, who at various times and in various ways spoke in time past to the fathers by the prophets, has in these last days spoken to us by His Son." — Hebrews 1:1–2 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Dios, habiendo hablado muchas veces y de muchas maneras en otro tiempo a los padres por los profetas, en estos postreros días nos ha hablado por el Hijo." — Hebreos 1:1–2 (RVG)

blocks.en: Day 2 — The Doctrinal Backbone (lean; full version in Systematic Theology Unit 1)
blocks.es_reference: Día 2 — El fundamento doctrinal (breve; versión completa en Teología Sistemática, Unidad 1)

blocks.en: Hold the doctrine clearly before shaping it into a sermon. Keep it compressed — point students to ST Unit 1 for the full treatment — but they cannot preach what they cannot summarize:
blocks.es_reference: Sostenga la doctrina con claridad antes de darle forma de sermón. Manténgala comprimida — remita a los alumnos a la Unidad 1 de TS para el tratamiento completo — pero no pueden predicar lo que no pueden resumir:

blocks.en: God must take the initiative. The starting point of all theology is not man’s search for God but God’s decision to make Himself known. The finite cannot reach the Infinite; if God had stayed silent, He could not be known. General and special revelation. General revelation, through nature, history, and conscience, shows that God exists, that He is powerful, and that man is accountable — but it cannot save. So God gave special revelation: His direct, redemptive self-disclosure in the history of Israel, in Jesus Christ, and in the Bible. Scripture as Absolute Authority. Rather than only defending what the Bible is not (not errant, not fallible), we affirm what it is: the final, supreme standard for all faith and practice. Inspiration is God causing Scripture through human authors; illumination is the Spirit opening it to the believer; transmission is God preserving it through the centuries.
blocks.es_reference: Dios debe tomar la iniciativa. El punto de partida de toda teología no es la búsqueda del hombre por Dios, sino la decisión de Dios de darse a conocer. Lo finito no puede alcanzar al Infinito; si Dios hubiera callado, no podría ser conocido. Revelación general y especial. La revelación general, por la naturaleza, la historia y la conciencia, muestra que Dios existe, que es poderoso y que el hombre es responsable — pero no puede salvar. Por eso Dios dio la revelación especial: su auto-revelación directa y redentora en la historia de Israel, en Jesucristo y en la Biblia. La Escritura como Autoridad Absoluta. En lugar de solo defender lo que la Biblia no es (no errante, no falible), afirmamos lo que es: la norma final y suprema para toda fe y práctica. La inspiración es Dios causando la Escritura por medio de autores humanos; la iluminación es el Espíritu abriéndola al creyente; la transmisión es Dios preservándola a través de los siglos.

blocks.en: Day 3 — The Homiletical Move
blocks.es_reference: Día 3 — El movimiento homilético

blocks.en: Now turn the doctrine into a sermon by the method of Unit 2. Subject: the Word of God. Interrogative: “In what forms does God speak His Word?” Keyword: forms (a plural noun — the outline grows from it). The keyword yields five points, and — this is the whole thesis of the course — each one stands on its own text:
blocks.es_reference: Ahora convierta la doctrina en sermón por el método de la Unidad 2. Tema: la Palabra de Dios. Interrogativo: “¿En qué formas habla Dios su Palabra?” Palabra clave: formas (un sustantivo plural — de él crece el bosquejo). La palabra clave produce cinco puntos, y — esta es toda la tesis del curso — cada uno se apoya en su propio texto:

blocks.en: Point (keyword: forms)Anchor text
blocks.es_reference: Punto (palabra clave: formas)Texto base

blocks.en: 1. The Living Word — Jesus ChristJohn 1:14
blocks.es_reference: 1. La Palabra Viva — JesucristoJuan 1:14

blocks.en: 2. The Preached (Prophetic) Word — proclamationRomans 10:14–17
blocks.es_reference: 2. La Palabra Predicada (Profética) — proclamaciónRomanos 10:14–17

blocks.en: 3. The Natural Word — creationPsalm 19:1; Romans 1:19–20
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Palabra Natural — la creaciónSalmo 19:1; Romanos 1:19–20

blocks.en: 4. The Written Word — the Bible2 Timothy 3:16–17
blocks.es_reference: 4. La Palabra Escrita — la Biblia2 Timoteo 3:16–17

blocks.en: 5. The Enacted Word — baptism and the Lord’s Supper1 Corinthians 11:26
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Palabra Actuada — el bautismo y la Cena del Señor1 Corintios 11:26

blocks.en: Five points, five texts, one subject. The preacher arranged them (topical, deductive), yet not one floats free of Scripture — which is exactly the answer to the charge that topical preaching is “just the preacher’s ideas.”
blocks.es_reference: Cinco puntos, cinco textos, un tema. El predicador los ordenó (tópico, deductivo), y sin embargo ni uno flota libre de la Escritura — que es exactamente la respuesta a la acusación de que la predicación tópica es “solo las ideas del predicador.”

blocks.en: Before fleshing out one point as a sermon, let each form be understood for what it is. These are not five competing words but five ways the one God makes Himself known.
blocks.es_reference: Antes de desarrollar un punto como sermón, entienda cada forma por lo que es. No son cinco palabras que compiten, sino cinco maneras en que el único Dios se da a conocer.

blocks.en: 1. The Living Word — Jesus Christ (John 1:14). Jesus is the living Word, the greatest revelation God ever gave of Himself. He is not one prophet among others but God’s own self-expression made flesh. Jesus said, “He who has seen Me has seen the Father” (John 14:9), and “I and My Father are one” (John 10:30). So the most perfect representation of God came into the world in the person of Jesus, the very Son of God. Every other form of the Word points to Him; He is the Word the others are about.
blocks.es_reference: 1. La Palabra Viva — Jesucristo (Juan 1:14). Jesús es la Palabra viva, la mayor revelación que Dios dio jamás de Sí mismo. No es un profeta más entre otros, sino la propia expresión de Dios hecha carne. Jesús dijo: “El que me ha visto a mí, ha visto al Padre” (Juan 14:9), y “Yo y el Padre uno somos” (Juan 10:30). Así que la representación más perfecta de Dios vino al mundo en la persona de Jesús, el mismo Hijo de Dios. Toda otra forma de la Palabra apunta a Él; Él es la Palabra de la que tratan las demás.

blocks.en: 2. The Preached (Prophetic) Word — proclamation (Romans 10:14–17). God has chosen to make His Word travel through human voices. “Faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God,” and “how shall they hear without a preacher?” The preacher does not invent the message; he carries it. When the Word of God is faithfully proclaimed, it is not merely a man speaking — God speaks through the proclamation, and faith is born in the hearer.
blocks.es_reference: 2. La Palabra Predicada (Profética) — proclamación (Romanos 10:14–17). Dios ha escogido hacer viajar su Palabra por voces humanas. “La fe viene por el oír, y el oír por la palabra de Dios,” y “¿cómo oirán sin haber quién les predique?” El predicador no inventa el mensaje; lo lleva. Cuando la Palabra de Dios se proclama con fidelidad, no es solo un hombre hablando — Dios habla por medio de la proclamación, y la fe nace en el oyente.

blocks.en: 3. The Natural Word — creation (Psalm 19:1; Romans 1:19–20). “The heavens declare the glory of God.” Creation itself is a form of God’s Word, telling every person in every language that God is real, powerful, and worthy. This natural revelation is enough to leave the whole world without excuse, but it is not enough to save — it can show that God is, but it cannot, by itself, show the way to Christ. It raises the question that only special revelation answers.
blocks.es_reference: 3. La Palabra Natural — la creación (Salmo 19:1; Romanos 1:19–20). “Los cielos cuentan la gloria de Dios.” La creación misma es una forma de la Palabra de Dios, diciendo a cada persona en cada idioma que Dios es real, poderoso y digno. Esta revelación natural basta para dejar al mundo entero sin excusa, pero no basta para salvar — puede mostrar que Dios existe, pero no puede, por sí sola, mostrar el camino a Cristo. Plantea la pregunta que solo la revelación especial responde.

blocks.en: 4. The Written Word — the Bible (2 Timothy 3:16–17). “All Scripture is given by inspiration of God.” Here the revelation is fixed, permanent, and reliable; what God spoke through prophets and apostles is preserved so that every generation can return to it and find the same truth. The written Word is where we go to test every other claim, including our own preaching; it is the standard that does not move.
blocks.es_reference: 4. La Palabra Escrita — la Biblia (2 Timoteo 3:16–17). “Toda la Escritura es dada por inspiración de Dios.” Aquí la revelación es fija, permanente y confiable; lo que Dios habló por los profetas y los apóstoles se conserva para que cada generación vuelva a ella y halle la misma verdad. La Palabra escrita es a donde vamos para probar toda otra afirmación, incluida nuestra propia predicación; es la norma que no se mueve.

blocks.en: 5. The Enacted Word — baptism and the Lord’s Supper (1 Corinthians 11:26). God also speaks in actions He commanded the church to perform. In baptism the gospel is pictured in water — death, burial, and resurrection; in the Lord’s Supper, “as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death till He comes.” These are the Word made visible, preaching the same gospel to the eye that the other forms preach to the ear.
blocks.es_reference: 5. La Palabra Actuada — el bautismo y la Cena del Señor (1 Corintios 11:26). Dios habla también en acciones que mandó a la iglesia realizar. En el bautismo el evangelio se retrata en agua — muerte, sepultura y resurrección; en la Cena del Señor, “todas las veces que comiereis este pan, y bebiereis esta copa, la muerte del Señor anunciáis hasta que él venga.” Son la Palabra hecha visible, predicando al ojo el mismo evangelio que las otras formas predican al oído.

blocks.en: Day 4 — Developing a Point (E-A-I) and an Illustration Bank
blocks.es_reference: Día 4 — Desarrollando un punto (E-A-I) y un banco de ilustraciones

blocks.en: A skeleton is not yet a sermon. Each point is fleshed out with Explanation, Application, and Illustration. Here is Point 1 (the Living Word, John 1:14) developed in full:
blocks.es_reference: Un esqueleto no es aún un sermón. Cada punto se desarrolla con Explicación, Aplicación e Ilustración. He aquí el Punto 1 (la Palabra Viva, Juan 1:14) desarrollado por completo:

blocks.en: Explanation of the text. “And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us.” A word is how a mind expresses itself; to hear God’s Word is to meet God’s mind. And the highest form of that Word is not ink on a page but a Person: in Jesus, God’s self-expression became flesh and moved into the neighborhood.
blocks.es_reference: Explicación del texto. “Y el Verbo se hizo carne y habitó entre nosotros.” Una palabra es cómo una mente se expresa; oír la Palabra de Dios es encontrar la mente de Dios. Y la forma más alta de esa Palabra no es tinta sobre una página, sino una Persona: en Jesús, la auto-expresión de Dios se hizo carne y vino a vivir entre nosotros.

blocks.en: Application of the text. So if you want to know what God is like, you look at Jesus. The hearer who finds God distant or frightening is invited to look at the face of Christ, for “he who has seen Me has seen the Father.” God is not hiding; He has come near.
blocks.es_reference: Aplicación del texto. Así que si quieres saber cómo es Dios, mira a Jesús. Al oyente que halla a Dios distante o temible se le invita a mirar el rostro de Cristo, porque “el que me ha visto a mí, ha visto al Padre.” Dios no se esconde; se ha acercado.

blocks.en: Illustration. A letter can tell you a great deal about someone, but it is not the same as the person walking through the door. The other forms of the Word are God’s letters; the Living Word is God Himself walking in.
blocks.es_reference: Ilustración. Una carta puede decirte mucho de alguien, pero no es lo mismo que la persona entrando por la puerta. Las otras formas de la Palabra son las cartas de Dios; la Palabra Viva es Dios mismo entrando.

blocks.en: The remaining four points are developed the same way. And revelation is unusually rich in illustration — use the bank:
blocks.es_reference: Los otros cuatro puntos se desarrollan igual. Y la revelación es inusualmente rica en ilustración — use el banco:

blocks.en: 💡 The Hotel Room: A traveler checks into a room at night; under the dim lamp it looks clean. Morning sunlight reveals the stains and dust. The room did not change — only the light did. God’s revelation does not create the truth about us; it shows what was always there. (From ST Unit 1.)
blocks.es_reference: 💡 La Habitación del Hotel: Un viajero se hospeda de noche; bajo la lámpara tenue la habitación parece limpia. La luz del sol por la mañana revela las manchas y el polvo. La habitación no cambió — solo cambió la luz. La revelación de Dios no crea la verdad sobre nosotros; muestra lo que siempre estuvo allí. (De la Unidad 1 de TS.)

blocks.en: 💡 The Letter and the Visit: see the Living-Word illustration above — the written word about a person versus the person arriving in the flesh.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 La Carta y la Visita: vea la ilustración de la Palabra Viva arriba — la palabra escrita sobre una persona frente a la persona que llega en carne.

blocks.en: 💡 The Power of a Fragment — Dr. Nikolai Alexandrenko: At Louisiana College there was a professor I came to know, Dr. Nikolai Alexandrenko. He had grown up an atheist in the Soviet Union and served as a paratroop officer in the Russian Army in the Second World War. Captured, he was held in a Nazi prisoner-of-war camp near Munich — and it was there, in the suffering and isolation of that camp, that he came upon a scrap of paper with a passage of Scripture on it. That fragment was not enough, by itself, to make him a Christian then and there; but it was enough to move an atheist to start searching, and that search did not end until he found Christ. He gave the rest of his life to the Word that had found him — earning his doctorates, teaching Scripture for decades, and helping found a seminary in Odessa to carry it back to his own people. A single fragment of God’s Word, found in a prison camp, was enough to set a man on the road from atheism to salvation. That is the power of the Word — which is why even a portion of it must never be despised, and why the searching heart is finally satisfied only by the full revelation of God in Christ.
blocks.es_reference: 💡 El Poder de un Fragmento — Dr. Nikolai Alexandrenko: En Louisiana College había un profesor que llegué a conocer, el Dr. Nikolai Alexandrenko. Se había criado ateo en la Unión Soviética y sirvió como oficial paracaidista en el Ejército Ruso en la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Capturado, fue recluido en un campo de prisioneros de guerra nazi cerca de Múnich — y fue allí, en el sufrimiento y el aislamiento de aquel campo, donde dio con un trozo de papel que tenía un pasaje de la Escritura. Ese fragmento no bastó, por sí solo, para hacerlo cristiano en aquel momento; pero bastó para mover a un ateo a comenzar a buscar, y esa búsqueda no terminó hasta que halló a Cristo. Dio el resto de su vida a la Palabra que lo había hallado — obteniendo sus doctorados, enseñando la Escritura por décadas, y ayudando a fundar un seminario en Odesa para llevarla de regreso a su propio pueblo. Un solo fragmento de la Palabra de Dios, hallado en un campo de prisioneros, bastó para poner a un hombre en el camino del ateísmo a la salvación. Ese es el poder de la Palabra — por lo cual ni siquiera una porción de ella debe despreciarse, y por lo cual el corazón que busca solo queda satisfecho con la revelación plena de Dios en Cristo.

blocks.en: Day 5 — Craft Notes and Summary
blocks.es_reference: Día 5 — Notas de oficio y resumen

blocks.en: Three cautions specific to preaching revelation. Do not preach a lecture on bibliology. The temptation is to spend the sermon on canon, manuscripts, and inspiration theories. Those belong in the lesson; the sermon aims at trust and obedience. Preach toward response. Let the doctrine’s own logic carry the arc: because God has spoken, He can be known; because He can be known, He can be trusted; because He can be trusted, He must be obeyed. That chain is the natural movement of the sermon toward the invitation. Preach it pictorially. Revelation is about a God who speaks and shows; the hotel room and the letter-versus-visit carry the truth into memory, which is the bridge to the narrative course.
blocks.es_reference: Tres advertencias propias de predicar la revelación. No prediques una clase de bibliología. La tentación es gastar el sermón en el canon, los manuscritos y las teorías de inspiración. Eso pertenece a la lección; el sermón apunta a la confianza y la obediencia. Predica hacia la respuesta. Deja que la propia lógica de la doctrina lleve el arco: porque Dios ha hablado, puede ser conocido; porque puede ser conocido, puede confiarse en Él; porque puede confiarse en Él, debe ser obedecido. Esa cadena es el movimiento natural del sermón hacia la invitación. Predica de forma pictórica. La revelación trata de un Dios que habla y muestra; la habitación del hotel y la carta-frente-a-la-visita llevan la verdad a la memoria, que es el puente al curso narrativo.

blocks.en: So Unit 3 has taken the first doctrine and run the whole method on it: a lean backbone from Systematic Theology, a subject and interrogative and keyword, five points each anchored to a text, one point developed by E-A-I, and an arc toward response. Unit 4 does the same with the doctrine of God.
blocks.es_reference: Así que la Unidad 3 ha tomado la primera doctrina y ha corrido todo el método sobre ella: un fundamento breve de la Teología Sistemática, un tema, un interrogativo y una palabra clave, cinco puntos cada uno anclado a un texto, un punto desarrollado por E-A-I, y un arco hacia la respuesta. La Unidad 4 hace lo mismo con la doctrina de Dios.

blocks.en: "The entrance of Your words gives light." — Psalm 119:130 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "La exposición de tus palabras alumbra." — Salmo 119:130 (RVG)

sa.prompt: Why does the preacher set the doctrine of revelation before the doctrine of God? What does it establish?
sa.model: The preacher sets revelation first because it establishes how God can be known at all, which must be settled before anything is said about who God is. The starting point of theology is not man’s search but God’s decision to make Himself known; the finite cannot reach the Infinite, so unless God has spoken, He cannot be known. Revelation is therefore the foundation and ground of every later doctrine, the reason any sermon on God, Christ, or salvation is possible. Establish that God has spoken, and every other doctrine has somewhere to stand.

sa.prompt: State the preacher’s pastoral aim in a sermon on revelation. What move should the hearer make?
sa.model: The pastoral aim is to move the hearer from religion as a human search to faith as a response to a God who has already spoken. The sermon must not leave people reaching up, guessing and hoping to find God on their own; it must turn them toward the God who has taken the initiative and made Himself known. The good news the hearer should grasp is not that we have found God but that God has come near and spoken, and the right response is to trust Him. So the sermon ends not in information but in faith.

sa.prompt: Lay out the homiletical move for preaching revelation: subject, interrogative, keyword, and how the points stay biblical.
sa.model: The subject is the Word of God. The interrogative asked of it is, in what forms does God speak His Word? The keyword that answers is forms, a plural noun from which the outline grows. The keyword yields five points, the Living, Preached, Natural, Written, and Enacted Word, and the points stay biblical because each one rests on its own text rather than on the preacher’s opinion. The preacher arranged the forms, which makes the sermon topical and deductive, yet the sermon is still the teaching of Scripture because every point is anchored to a passage.

sa.prompt: Name the five forms of the Word of God and the text under each.
sa.model: The Word of God comes in five forms, each on its own text. The Living Word is Jesus Christ, who became flesh, on John 1:14. The Preached or Prophetic Word is the proclamation of God’s truth, on Romans 10:14–17. The Natural Word is God’s revelation through creation, on Psalm 19:1 and Romans 1:19–20. The Written Word is the Bible, on 2 Timothy 3:16–17. And the Enacted Word is baptism and the Lord’s Supper, where the truth is acted out, on 1 Corinthians 11:26. Five forms, five texts, one subject.

sa.prompt: Develop the Living Word (John 1:14) as a sermon point using Explanation, Application, and Illustration.
sa.model: The Explanation of the text is that a word expresses a mind, and the Word became flesh, so in Jesus God’s own self-expression took on flesh and dwelt among us; the highest form of God’s Word is a Person. The Application is that if you want to know what God is like, you look at Jesus, for he who has seen Him has seen the Father; the hearer who finds God distant is invited to look at the face of Christ, because God has come near and is not hiding. The Illustration is that a letter tells you much about someone, but it is not the same as the person walking through the door; the other forms are God’s letters, and the Living Word is God Himself arriving in the flesh.

sa.prompt: Explain the difference between general and special revelation. What can each do, and what can general revelation NOT do?
sa.model: General revelation is God’s disclosure through nature, history, and conscience, available to all people; it shows that God exists, that He is powerful, and that man is accountable to Him. What it cannot do is save; it gives awareness but not the way of forgiveness. Special revelation is God’s direct, redemptive self-disclosure in the history of Israel, in the person and work of Jesus Christ, and in the Bible. Because general revelation can make people accountable but cannot bring them to salvation, God gave special revelation, which alone makes Christ and the gospel known.

sa.prompt: Why does the course prefer “Absolute Authority” over terms like inerrancy and infallibility?
sa.model: Terms like inerrancy and infallibility have value, but they are framed as negatives, telling us what the Bible is not, not errant and not fallible. The course prefers Absolute Authority because it is a positive affirmation of what Scripture is and how we live under it. It moves the conversation from technical debates about the mechanics of the text to the practical reality of submitting to God’s Word. To say the Bible has absolute authority is to confess that it is the final, supreme standard for all faith and practice, so that we do not stand in judgment of the Word; the Word stands in judgment of us.

These three describe how God gave, opens, and keeps His Word. Inspiration is God causing Scripture to be written while working through human authors, so that the text itself is God-breathed. Illumination is the ongoing work of the Holy Spirit enabling the believer to understand and apply what was written, since knowledge alone is insufficient without the Spirit opening our eyes. Transmission is God’s preservation of His Word through the centuries by canonization, manuscript copying, and translation, so that what reaches us is reliably what He gave. Inspiration produced the Word, illumination opens it to the reader, and transmission has preserved it.

sa.prompt: Give two cautions for preaching revelation well, and explain why the sermon should reach toward response.
sa.model: One caution is not to preach a lecture on bibliology, spending the whole sermon on canon, manuscripts, and inspiration theories; those belong in the lesson, while the sermon aims at trust and obedience. A second caution is to preach pictorially, using illustrations like the hotel room so the truth lodges in memory. The sermon should reach toward response because the doctrine’s own logic forms an arc: because God has spoken, He can be known; because known, trusted; because trusted, obeyed. That chain carries the hearer naturally to the invitation, so revelation is preached not for information but for a response of faith and obedience.

sa.prompt: Summarize how Unit 3 turns the doctrine of revelation into a sermon, from backbone to arc.
sa.model: Unit 3 takes the first doctrine and runs the whole method on it. It begins with a lean doctrinal backbone drawn from Systematic Theology: God must take the initiative, general revelation cannot save, and Scripture is the absolute authority. Then it makes the homiletical move: the subject is the Word of God, the interrogative asks in what forms God speaks, and the keyword forms yields five points, each anchored to its own text. One point, the Living Word, is developed by Explanation, Application, and Illustration to show how flesh is put on the skeleton. Finally the sermon bends toward response along the chain spoken, known, trusted, obeyed. Backbone, method, worked example, and arc to the invitation: that is the template every doctrine unit follows.
